title: Decant an aged wine off its sediment: pour slowly and stop when the sediment reaches the bottle's shoulder
context: Sommeliers, waiters and bartenders decant aged red wine at the table (O*NET 35-3031.00, Waiters and Waitresses; 35-3011.00, Bartenders). An old red throws a sediment of tannins and pigment that settles on the bottle's bottom once it has stood upright, and the point of decanting is to pour the clear wine off it: tip the bottle slowly over the decanter with a light or a white surface behind the neck, watch the sediment creep along the bottle toward the neck once most of the wine has gone, and stop as it reaches the shoulder, leaving the last few centimeters of wine with the sediment in the bottle, which then goes back down upright. Pouring to the last drop, as with any other bottle, puts the gritty, bitter sediment in the decanter and spoils the wine, while stopping far too early wastes it, and the only cue for when to stop is the dark layer moving inside the bottle.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A clear (flint) glass wine bottle, 4.8 cm across and 13.1 cm tall with 220 g mass, stands upright centered at x 23, y -12: an 8.9 cm cylindrical body, a 1.2 cm shoulder and a 3 cm neck 2.1 cm across with a cut dark red foil capsule just below the open mouth (1.7 cm inside). It holds 120 mL: a 12 mL layer of dark sediment (with the wine trapped in it) lying 0.8 cm deep on its bottom, shown near black, under 108 mL of clear red wine, shown ruby. An empty clear glass decanter with 600 g mass stands centered at x 33, y -1: a wide base 11.6 cm across and 4.5 cm tall narrowing to a neck 6.6 cm across (6 cm inside), 8.5 cm tall in all. A white card 16 cm wide and 16 cm tall stands on its own 5 cm deep foot (600 g in all) centered at x 29, y 6.8, just beyond the decanter on the robot's left and facing the right arm, so that a bottle tipped over the decanter is seen against white from the right wrist camera, as a sommelier holds the neck over a candle. Nothing else is on the table. The liquids are drawn inside each vessel and as a stream while pouring. Upright, the sediment lies on the bottle's bottom; tipped past 70 degrees, the wine is drawn running toward the neck and the sediment as a dark band across the bottle at its front, which moves from the bottom toward the shoulder as the sediment slides, and for the last quarter of its slide a dark edge grows into the shoulder around the wine there.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run and tracks the liquids in mL. The score is 0, irreversibly, if the bottle or the decanter is knocked over, leaning more than 45 degrees for 2 control steps in a row with no gripper holding it. It is 0 if less than 10.8 mL (10 percent) of the clear wine is in the decanter, which covers doing nothing and pouring anywhere else, and 0 if more than 1 mL of sediment is in the decanter, which is what pouring on after the sediment reaches the shoulder does (1 mL is a twelfth of the sediment, enough to cloud the wine). The sediment begins to slide toward the neck only once the bottle leans past 75 degrees, where the crust lies on the bottle's lower wall instead of its floor, with less than 50 mL of wine left over it (under half the wine), when the wine no longer covers the crust along that wall; it then takes 4 s to reach the shoulder with no stream and as little as 0.8 s under a full stream, stops when the bottle is tipped back under 75 degrees, and once at the shoulder pours with the wine and, past 85 degrees, runs out on its own at 2 mL/s. Tipped past 93 degrees, with the neck below horizontal, the pour glugs: air gulps back up the neck and churns the sediment up toward the shoulder, faster the steeper it is (from the floor to the shoulder in 0.5 s at 103 degrees), so a steep flip held for a counted time fails however it is timed. The demo peaks at about 87 degrees. With sediment kept out, more than 3 mL of liquid spilled or splashed in all scores 0.25 (a stain on the cloth rather than drips), and a stream falling more than 10 cm from the lip to the decanter's rim splashes a quarter of itself out. Otherwise 10.8 to 64.8 mL of wine in the decanter scores 0.5 (stopped far too early) and at least 64.8 mL (60 percent) scores 0.75: the bar sits 6.8 mL past the point where the sediment starts to move, so a pour that stops before the sediment has visibly moved falls short, while a slow pour stopped as the sediment nears the shoulder puts in about 65 to 77 mL and leaves about a third of the wine with the sediment, as decanting an old bottle does. It scores 1.0 when the bottle is also standing upright within 10 degrees, still, on the table and let go, with both arms home (each tool point within 3 cm of where it started and still), and 0.9 with an arm not home. Success is a full score held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial, weigh the decanter, let it stand 5 minutes and draw off its bottom into a graduated syringe to measure the settled sediment, and weigh a white cloth under both vessels for spills.
reset_notes: Empty and rinse the decanter and bottle, put 12 mL of the sediment stand-in (fine used coffee grounds in red-dyed water) in the bottle, add 108 mL of red-dyed water down the side without stirring, and let the bottle stand upright on its spot for 10 minutes so the grounds settle. Set the decanter on its spot and replace the white cloth.
fidelity: About 0.45 scale of a 750 mL bottle, holding 120 mL, with no fluid simulation: the bottle holds what fits below its lip at its tilt and pours the rest straight down at a capped rate. The pour and the sediment's slide run about 6 times faster than a real decant of about a minute. The drawn liquid fills the bottle along its axis rather than lying level, the clear glass is drawn as thin rings, and the white card stands in for a candle.
